The interview after the march
Saturday, 13 May 2034. After the “Tree March”, which brought three thousand people to Lyon town hall, a radio journalist interviews Inès, 16, the organiser.
Inès, you’re sixteen and you’ve just brought together three thousand people. Why this march?
Because in my neighbourhood eleven trees have been cut down in ten years, and not one has been replanted. Yet every tree cut down raises the temperature of the street.
Was it last year’s heatwave that made up your mind?
Yes. It was so hot that children were fainting during rehearsals. And for lack of shade, elderly people could no longer go out.
What exactly are you asking for?
We’re asking the city to replant a tree for every tree cut down, so that our streets are still liveable in twenty years.
The mayor has replied to you, I believe?
Yes. He said he had heard our message, and that the city would replant two trees for every tree cut down, from next year.
During your speech, you asked the crowd to be quiet. Why?
So that people could hear the sound of a city without trees: nothing. Not a single bird. Silence can be stronger than a speech; I learnt that in an orchestra.
And the three thousand little trees you were carrying?
They’ll be planted tomorrow, so that the march goes on even after we’ve gone. That’s the most important thing: it’s not that we want to make noise, it’s that we want to leave something behind.

1. Review: cause (ch. 83)

Nuance matters: “grâce à” for a good result, “à cause de” for a bad one, “en raison de” in official register.
2. Review: consequence and purpose (ch. 84)

“De sorte que” has both meanings: + indicative = consequence (“de sorte que la marche a continué”), + subjunctive = purpose (“de sorte que la marche continue”).

Le banc d’Antoine

In the spring of 2034, Inès was sixteen, and she had decided to change the world. Or at least Lyon. Since the summer of the heatwave, she had talked about nothing but trees. She had read all of Dr Lefèvre’s reports, all the articles on heat islands, all the books in the lycée library on global warming. And she had noticed something that drove her mad: in her neighbourhood, eleven trees had been cut down in ten years, and not a single one had been replanted.

She had talked about it with Claire Vasseur, who had advised her to do what she did best: speak. So Inès had organised a march. Not a demonstration, she had pointed out, a march: “The Tree March”. On Saturday 13 May, at ten o’clock, the participants would leave from the Salle Hélène Morel, each with a young tree in a pot, and walk to the town hall to ask for a tree to be replanted for every tree cut down.

That left the question of the trees. Where could they find hundreds of young trees, and who would pay for them? Dr Lefèvre found the answer: a nursery in the Drôme that had to get rid of thousands of unsold saplings every spring, for lack of space. It gave them free, on condition that they were planted within the week. Amina drew up the distribution spreadsheet. One tree per registered participant. She ordered two hundred. Three thousand were needed.

Clémence had come from Paris for the march, by train, with her violin and a little lime tree in a pot. She was seventeen now. Her father, the minister, had asked her not to show herself too much in front of the cameras, for fear he would be accused of using his daughter. Clémence had replied that on that day she wasn’t his daughter, but Inès’s friend. She had marched in the front row, beside her, the whole way.

She was hoping for fifty people. Three thousand came. The children of the La Duchère orchestra, of course, with their instruments. The pupils of Inès’s lycée. “The Thursday Ducks”, every one of them, with Bernard Delorme in front on his trumpet. Whole families, grandparents, pushchairs. And hundreds of little potted trees, limes, maples, oaks, moving through the streets of Lyon like a walking forest.

Nadia walked beside her daughter, her flute in one hand and a little oak in the other. She had taken the night off, for the second time in her life, to be there. She said nothing. She watched Inès talk to journalists, police officers, passers-by, with a confidence she had never seen in her, and wondered how the child who had been afraid to speak three years earlier had become this young woman. Sami carried Nadia’s tree when she got tired.

Rose-Hélène had done the whole march on her father’s shoulders, with her maple in her arms. She could see everything from up there: the thousands of little trees moving forward, the instruments, the signs. On hers, she had drawn a tree half green, half black. Passers-by asked her what it meant. She answered that it was a tree in Corsica that had been very thirsty, and that it was better now.

In front of the town hall, on the Place des Terreaux, Inès climbed onto an improvised platform made of wooden crates. She spoke for six minutes, without notes. The next day, the papers reported her speech. She had said she hadn’t come to accuse anyone. She had explained that every tree cut down raised the temperature of the street by one degree. And she had asked the officials whether they wanted their grandchildren to live in an oven.

Then she had done something nobody expected. She had asked the crowd to be quiet. Three thousand people fell silent on the Place des Terreaux. For about eight bars there was no sound except the pigeons and the Bartholdi fountain. Then Inès said into the microphone: “That’s the sound of a city without trees. Not a single bird. Nothing.” And she stepped down from the platform.

The mayor came out of the town hall ten minutes later. He told the journalists he had heard the message. He announced that the city would replant two trees for every tree cut down, starting the following year. Then he went over to Inès and asked her where she had learnt to speak like that. Inès replied that she had learnt at the Odéon, but above all in an orchestra, where she had been taught that silence was sometimes stronger than music.

The same day, in Grenoble, Mrs Faure had organised her own march, much smaller: two hundred people, on rue des Tanneurs, with Joseph, Mathis and his drums, and Mrs Rey in a wheelchair pushed by her great-nephew. They had planted fifty trees along the old glove factory. That evening, Mrs Faure sent Bernard Delorme a photo with a single word: “Competition.” Bernard Delorme replied with three exclamation marks.

That evening, Inès came home exhausted, her hands black with earth, her voice hoarse from talking too much. Her mother had made her favourite dish. Inès fell asleep at the table in the middle of the meal, her head on her arms. Nadia watched her sleep for a long time. Then she took her phone and sent a message to Claire Vasseur: “Thank you for teaching her to speak. I didn’t know how.” Claire replied: “She’s the one who taught us.”

The three thousand little trees were not lost. Dr Lefèvre, who had marched with them, had planned what came next. On the Sunday they were planted in every free space the city had agreed to give up: along the tram lines, in school playgrounds, on the banks of the Rhône. It took the whole day. Rose-Hélène planted hers, a little maple, next to her school’s silver lime. She named it Antoine.

At La Duchère, nobody had forgotten the previous summer. In April, thanks to a grant obtained by Amina, the city had installed four large rainwater tanks at the foot of the tower blocks, so that the lime tree by the Salle Hélène Morel would never again lack water, even in the worst drought. Amina had calculated that the tanks could store twelve thousand litres. She had added that this was slightly more than the air-conditioner water of the previous summer. To be on the safe side.

Amina, in fact, had changed a lot in the past year. She smiled more often. She had been late for work twice, which had never happened in six years. And on Thursday evenings, after rehearsal, she no longer walked back alone towards the station. She walked towards Croix-Rousse with Mr Vidal, who carried his violin in one hand and Amina’s triangle in the other.

Nobody dared ask them any questions. They had never held hands in public. They still used “vous” in front of others, out of habit, then switched to “tu” as soon as they thought nobody could hear. “The Thursday Ducks” group counted the days, the glances, the shared coffees. Bernard Delorme had even organised a secret bet: the date on which “something would finally happen”. He had bet on Christmas. He lost.

What nobody knew was that Mr Vidal had asked someone’s advice a week before the concert. Not Julien, nor Théo, nor Isabelle. Rose-Hélène. He had found her on the landing one Sunday, playing hopscotch. He had asked her, very seriously, how you asked someone something very important. Rose-Hélène had thought about it. Then she had said you first had to play three notes and wait for an answer.

Mr Vidal had written the advice in his grey notebook. He had asked what you did if the other person didn’t answer. Rose-Hélène had said that never happened, if you had chosen the right person. Then she had added, going back to her hopscotch, that he could also make a spreadsheet, because everyone knew Amina loved spreadsheets. Mr Vidal had smiled. He had said he had already thought of that.

Because something did happen on Thursday 22 June, at the Thursday orchestra’s end-of-season concert, in a packed Salle Hélène Morel. The orchestra had played the march, the Romanian tune, two new pieces, and to finish Henri’s waltz, with Amina’s triangle in the middle of the silence. The audience was applauding. Théo was bowing. And at that very moment Mr Vidal stood up in the back row and asked to speak.

Théo, surprised, held out the microphone. Mr Vidal didn’t take it. He took a sheet of paper folded in four out of the pocket of his grey suit. He unfolded it. It was a spreadsheet. He showed it to the audience, then read it aloud in his low, precise magistrate’s voice. The spreadsheet had two columns. The first was headed “Advantages”. The second, “Disadvantages”. There were twelve lines in the first column.

He read them one by one. “She counts better than I do. She never takes sugar in her coffee, so we will never run out. She taught me that a single note could be enough. She deleted the column of my train times.” The audience laughed. Amina, in the front row next to Mrs Roux, had turned scarlet. She was holding her triangle in both hands like a shield. She no longer moved.

Then he came to the second column. He announced that he had looked for disadvantages for three months, with all the rigour a magistrate of the Court of Audit was capable of. He had found only one. He read it: “She hasn’t said yes yet.” Then he folded the sheet again, looked at Amina, and asked her, in front of five hundred people, whether she would kindly correct this single irregularity.

There was a silence. A real silence, longer than eight bars. Amina stood up. She crossed the hall, slowly, to the back row. She took the sheet from Mr Vidal’s hands. She unfolded it. She read the spreadsheet carefully, line by line, checking every figure, as she would have done at the office. The whole hall held its breath. Then she took a pen out of her bag.

She crossed out the only line in the “Disadvantages” column. Beside it she wrote a single word in capital letters: “CORRECTED”. Then she handed the sheet back to Mr Vidal. She said, very calmly, that according to her calculations the spreadsheet was now perfectly balanced. Mr Vidal looked at the sheet. He said he agreed with her calculations. And the Salle Hélène Morel exploded.

Bernard Delorme played a triumphant fanfare on his trumpet, so loudly that the panes of the skylight shook. The baker beat her drum. Nadia was crying into her flute. Mrs Roux, in her wheelchair, clapped and shouted “At last!”. And Rose-Hélène, sitting on the floor in the front row, played the three notes on her harmonica, over and over, without stopping, because she didn’t know what else to do.

Later, at the buffet, Julien asked Amina why she had taken so long to answer in front of the spreadsheet. Amina explained that she had checked the sums. Bertrand had written that there were twelve advantages, but there were only eleven on the sheet. She had found the mistake. Julien asked what she had done. Amina smiled. She said she had decided not to report it. For once.

The next day, at the office, Amina arrived on time, as always. She opened her computer, as always. Then she did something she had never done: she called Julien into her office, closed the door, and instead of crying, as the three other times, she burst out laughing. A huge, uncontrollable laugh that lasted five minutes. The whole team heard it through the door. Nobody dared go in.

The wedding was set for October, at the Croix-Rousse town hall. Amina made a spreadsheet of the guests, a spreadsheet of the budget and a spreadsheet of the songs. Mr Vidal asked to add a column. He didn’t say what for. That same evening, in “The Thursday Ducks” group, Bernard Delorme announced that he had lost his bet and would provide the champagne. There were five hundred and forty messages.

A week later, on Friday 30 June, it was Rose-Hélène’s last day of nursery school. It was also the last day for Mrs Chevalier, who was retiring after thirty-eight years of teaching. She had kept Rose-Hélène for three years, which had never been seen at the school. She had told the head she wanted to end her career with the little girl who had taught her the most beautiful music lesson of her life.

The children had prepared a surprise in secret with the parents. At the end of the day, in the playground, around the silver lime and the little maple, the twenty-four top-section children lined up. Lucas gave the signal. And they whistled Henri’s waltz. All twenty-four of them. For three years, Rose-Hélène had taught the whole class to whistle, one by one, at every break. Even Lucas could do it now. Almost in tune.

Mrs Chevalier listened to them without moving, her hand over her mouth. At the moment of silence, the twenty-four children stopped together. Then, instead of carrying on, they turned to her. Rose-Hélène stepped forward. She held out a little cardboard box. Inside was a new harmonica, bought with the whole class’s money, and a label written by Rose-Hélène herself: “For you. The silence is yours now.”

Mrs Chevalier took the harmonica out of the box. She didn’t know how to play it. She put it to her lips anyway, and blew. A note came out, just one, out of tune, trembling. The twenty-four children applauded as if it were a concert. Then they whistled the rest of the waltz, to the end. Mrs Chevalier was crying. She said later it was the most beautiful day of her thirty-eight-year career. And the saddest.

In July, a photo arrived from Bucharest. It was Mr Petrescu in his workshop, next to Viorica’s piano, completely dismantled, but with a brand-new soundboard of pale spruce that gleamed under the lamp. In the photo, Viorica was sitting next to him on a wooden chair, in her black coat despite the heat. She was holding her father’s letter. Under the photo, Andrei had written: “One more year.”

In August, Nathalie and Yves Le Goff came to spend a week in Lyon. Yves was ninety and had a new cane, made of driftwood, which Nathalie had carved for him. Nathalie had tanned cheeks and hands roughened by ropes: Yves was teaching her to sail on an old sailing boat. They made galettes for the whole building on rue d’Austerlitz. Isabelle said her mother would have loved to see it.

The summer of 2034 was hot, but less so than the year before. There were two short heatwaves, in July and August, and lots of storms. Thanks to the tanks, the La Duchère lime tree never lacked water. Thanks to the three thousand trees from the march, some streets in Lyon were already a little cooler. And thanks to Marie-Ange, who still sent a photo every week, Rose-Hélène watched the Corsican lime tree turn green, on its left side, all summer long.

On 4 September, Rose-Hélène started primary school, in the big school on the other side of the playground. Her new teacher was called Mr Bernard. He was a tall, bearded, calm man who played the guitar. On the first day he asked the pupils to introduce themselves and say what they liked. When it was Rose-Hélène’s turn, she took Henri’s harmonica out of her school bag and asked whether it needed negotiating.

Mr Bernard looked at the harmonica, then at the little girl. He had heard about her, of course. The whole school had heard about her. He thought for a moment. Then he proposed a deal: the harmonica would stay in its box, in her bag, during lessons. But on Friday afternoons, at the end of the week, Rose-Hélène would be allowed to play three notes for the whole class. Rose-Hélène asked whether she could whistle the next three as well. Mr Bernard said yes.

At the end of August, Amina finally found out what the mysterious column Mr Vidal had added to the wedding spreadsheet contained. It was headed “Silence”. For each moment of the ceremony, he had noted the exact length of a silence to be observed: eight bars after the “yes”, eight bars before the meal, eight bars at the end. Amina checked the calculations. They were correct. She changed nothing.

On Saturday 9 September, the whole family took the boat to Corsica. The new village school was opening its doors on the Monday, and the mayor had organised a small opening ceremony on the Sunday morning. Ioana was invited, with Hugo, who had drawn the plans, and Julien, on behalf of the network. Rose-Hélène had been invited personally, by a letter from Marie-Ange written in pencil: “Come. The bench is waiting for you.”

On the night boat, Hugo didn’t sleep. It was the first time he was going to see a building he had designed, completely built, lived in, ready for use. He was twenty-nine. He had drawn dozens of projects, but none had ever meant so much to him. He spent the night on deck, looking at the sea, holding a printed photo of the façade. Ioana found him there at sunrise. She didn’t say anything to him. She brought him a coffee.

The village had changed. The hills were still black, but green was already appearing here and there: grasses, bushes, little pines growing back between the burnt trunks. Most of the houses had been repaired. And on the square, next to the wash house and the fountain, stood the new school: a simple building of pale stone, with a red-tiled roof and, in the middle, the big picture window of the music room, facing the lime tree.

And the lime tree was there. Half green, half black. On the left side, the one that hadn’t burnt, the branches were covered in thick, shiny leaves that moved in the wind. On the right side, the branches stayed black and bare, stretched towards the sky like arms. Dr Lefèvre had said it would stay like that for years. Perhaps forever. Rose-Hélène looked at it for a long time. She said it was beautiful like that.

In front of the picture window, facing the tree, was the bench. A grey stone bench, carved from a single block by the stonemason from Corte, simple and heavy. On the backrest an inscription had been engraved, in Corsican and in French. In Corsican, Marie-Ange read: “U bancu d’Antone”. Below, in French, was a sentence the mayor had chosen, one Antoine had said to a neighbour the previous summer: “You don’t know that. Neither do I. So I water it.”

On the Saturday evening, the night before the opening, Marie-Ange invited the whole family to dinner, with Paul Santoni, the mayor and the site foreman. She had cooked Antoine’s favourite dishes: chestnut soup, ewe’s cheese, brocciu fritters. At the end of the meal she raised her glass towards the window, from which you could see the square and the tree in the night. She said something in Corsican that Paul Santoni refused to translate. He said it was between them.

On Sunday 10 September, at eleven o’clock, the whole village gathered on the square. The mayor gave a short speech. He recalled that a year earlier, all that was left of the school was four blackened walls. He thanked the four thousand donors, the city of Lyon, the Fabre & Popescu firm, and Hugo, who went bright red. Then he said that the best architect of this school had never drawn a plan. His name was Antoine. And he had drawn with a bucket.

Then he asked Rose-Hélène to be the first to sit on the bench. She stepped forward, very serious, in her Sunday dress, Henri’s harmonica in her hand. She sat down in the middle of the stone bench, facing the tree. It was a quarter past eleven. The September sun was falling on the square. And the shade of the lime tree was falling on the bench. But only on the left half. The right half was in the sun.

Rose-Hélène noticed straight away. She looked at her left hand, in the shade. Her right hand, in the sun. Then she moved right over to the left end of the bench, entirely in the shade, and left the right half empty, in the sun. Marie-Ange asked her why she was moving over. Rose-Hélène replied, as if it were obvious: “The place in the sun is for Antoine. He’s waited in the shade long enough.”

Nobody said anything. Marie-Ange crossed herself. Then she sat down next to Rose-Hélène, in the shade too, leaving the sunny half empty. Then one of the other two singers sat on the ground in front of the bench. Then Paul Santoni. Then the village children, the ones who would start at the new school the next day. Soon the whole square was sitting around the bench. And the sunny half stayed empty.

Then Rose-Hélène played the three notes, towards the empty place, towards the tree, towards the black side of the branches. Then she whistled the next three. And for the first time, it was the village children who answered. Paul Santoni had taught them the waltz all summer, in secret, for the opening. They played it on recorders, tambourines and an old guitar, in front of the picture window of their new music room.

At the third verse, they stopped. Eight bars of silence. And in that silence, on the village square, something happened that everyone who was there told afterwards, each in their own way. A gust of wind came down from the mountain. The leaves on the green side all quivered at the same moment. And the black branches on the burnt side creaked softly, once. Like an old man sitting back down.

Marie-Ange said later that she had felt someone sit down beside her, on the sunny half. Paul Santoni said it was the wind. The mayor said he didn’t know. Hugo said the stone had moved because of the heat. Julien said nothing. And Rose-Hélène, when she was asked what she thought, replied that Antoine had come to sit in the sun, of course, since his place had been kept for him.

The next day, Monday 11 September, at half past eight, the new school bell rang for the first time. Seventeen children came into the playground. The first lesson of the day, by the mayor’s decision, was a music lesson. Paul Santoni opened the room in the middle of the building. The children sat facing the big picture window. And through the glass, in the middle of the square, they could see the lime tree. And the bench.

Before they left, Paul Santoni gave Rose-Hélène a USB stick. He had recorded the village children’s rehearsals all summer and had put the final version of the waltz, played in front of the bench, on the stick. At the end he had also added a very old recording, found in the town hall archives: Antoine, aged forty, in 1977, singing with two other shepherds. Rose-Hélène held the stick to her chest the whole journey.

In the cabin that night, Julien and his daughter listened to the 1977 recording with one earphone each. Antoine’s voice was young, strong, confident, almost unrecognisable. He was singing the lowest part, the one that carried the other two. Rose-Hélène listened to the end without moving. Then she said Antoine had the voice of a big tree. Julien said that was exactly it.

Rose-Hélène was already on the boat home. She had school too, in Lyon, with Mr Bernard, and she didn’t want to miss Friday afternoon. On deck, she asked her father whether the tree would one day have leaves on both sides. Julien repeated what Dr Lefèvre had said: that it was possible, but it would take years. Rose-Hélène said it didn’t matter. She would come back every summer to see.

Then she took out of her bag the three keys she now kept together on the same blue ribbon: the one to Odile’s flat, the one to Antoine’s sheepfold, and a little new key that Mrs Chevalier had given her on her last day of nursery school, the one to the box of her new harmonica. Rose-Hélène said that when she was grown up, she would have lots of doors to open. Julien said that was exactly the point.

On Friday 15 September, at four o’clock, in Mr Bernard’s first-year class, Rose-Hélène was allowed to play her three notes for the first time. She stood up, took Henri’s harmonica out of its box, and played, in front of twenty-six six-year-olds who didn’t know the story yet. Then she whistled the next three. Then she waited. Nobody knew what to do.

What Rose-Hélène didn’t know was that someone had come to watch this first Friday. At the back of the classroom, sitting on a little child’s chair, was Mrs Chevalier. Mr Bernard had invited her, in secret. She had been retired for two and a half months. She had brought her new harmonica, the one the class had given her. She still couldn’t play it. But she had it in her hand.

Then, at the back of the classroom, Mr Bernard picked up his guitar. He had learnt the waltz over the summer, in secret, like Paul Santoni, like Mrs Chevalier, like so many others before him. He played the rest, softly, up to the silence. Eight bars. Twenty-six children falling silent without knowing why. And in the middle of the silence, a small voice in the front row whistled a note. Just one. In tune. It was Lucas.

The open letter Inès sent to the mayor and the newspapers a week before the march. It is a model DELF B2 argumentative letter. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Lettre ouverte à Monsieur le Maire de Lyon
Dear Mr Mayor, I am writing to you on behalf of the young people of La Duchère, who last summer lived through the worst heatwave in our city’s history.
As you know, it was so hot that children fainted during our orchestra’s rehearsals. For lack of shade, elderly people stayed shut indoors for nine weeks.

Yet in ten years, eleven trees have been cut down in our neighbourhood, and not one has been replanted. Dr Lefèvre, the city botanist, explained to us that every tree cut down raised the temperature of the street by one degree.
Given that heatwaves will become more and more frequent because of global warming, our streets risk becoming unliveable, to the point that some neighbourhoods could be abandoned.
That is why we ask the city to commit to replanting a tree for every tree cut down, so that our children can still walk in the shade in twenty years.
It is not that we wish to accuse you. We want to build together with you. We therefore invite you to our march on Saturday 13 May. Yours faithfully, — Inès, sixteen, La Duchère
